articles.title: 21 million supply cap
articles.caption: Bitcoin's fixed maximum supply
articles.short: The rule that no more than 21 million bitcoins will ever exist.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins, and the block reward halves every 210,000 blocks.[1] Satoshi set out the schedule in the v0.1 release notes, “with the amount cut in half every 4 years” (release notes), and repeated it in the 0.3 announcement: “Bitcoin's total circulation is limited to 21 million coins.” (the announcement).

When users worried that so few coins could not serve the world, he pointed to divisibility: “Eventually at most only 21 million coins for 6.8 billion people in the world if it really gets huge. But don't worry, there are another 6 decimal places that aren't shown” (the post). See Satoshi (unit).

On lost coins he wrote: “Lost coins only make everyone else's coins worth slightly more. Think of it as a donation to everyone.” (the post).

When Mike Hearn asked in 2009 where “24 million coins” came from, Satoshi replied that “there's only going to be 21 million coins for the whole world” (the emails).
refs: Bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Adam Back
articles.caption: Inventor of Hashcash
articles.short: British cryptographer whose Hashcash the white paper cites.
articles.label: adam-back
articles.lead: Adam Back is a British cryptographer and cypherpunk who invented Hashcash in 1997,[1] a proof-of-work scheme for spam control.[2] Bitcoin's white paper cites it,[3] and Back was one of the first two people Satoshi is known to have emailed.[1]

sections.html: On 20 August 2008 Satoshi, writing from satoshi@anonymousspeech.com, asked Back to confirm a citation: “I'm getting ready to release a paper that references your Hashcash paper and I wanted to make sure I have the citation right.” He described the paper under its working title, Electronic Cash Without a Trusted Third Party. Back replied that the citation looked fine and suggested Wei Dai's b-money proposal. Satoshi answered: “I wasn't aware of the b-money page, but my ideas start from exactly that point.” (the emails). nakamoto-archive keeps a copy of the exchange.[4]

Back co-founded Blockstream in 2014. He has been named as a possible Satoshi several times: by the Financial Times in 2016, and in April 2026 by a New York Times investigation by John Carreyrou, which pointed to less common phrases, shared niche interests and the timing of Satoshi's last communication and Back's first public comment on Bitcoin. Back denied it again.[1] See Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto.

Bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Bitcoin Core
articles.caption: The continuation of Satoshi's client
articles.short: The software descended from Satoshi's original client.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin Core is the software Satoshi first published under the name “Bitcoin”; it took the name Bitcoin Core with version 0.9.0 in 2014.[1] Its GitHub repository holds the full history back to the SourceForge era, including all of Satoshi's commits.[2]

After Satoshi stepped back, Gavin Andresen led development until Wladimir J. van der Laan took over as lead maintainer on 8 April 2014.[1] Satoshi's last commit is SVN revision 202 (“get external ip from irc”); the 203 commits listed under his name are in the Commits folder of Satoshi Mail (open Commits).
refs: Bitcoin Core, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
bitcoin/bitcoin, Bitcoin Core source repository, GitHub.

articles.title: Bitcoin Pizza Day
articles.caption: 22 May 2010
articles.short: The 22 May 2010 purchase of two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin Pizza Day marks 22 May 2010, when Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, worth about $41 at the time.[1] It was the first known commercial transaction using bitcoin, later celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day.[2]

A few days earlier Satoshi had written to Hanyecz asking him to slow down his GPU mining, which was earning him far more coins than CPU miners could (the email).
refs: History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Bitcoin v0.1
articles.caption: The first release, January 2009
articles.short: The first release of the Bitcoin software, for Windows, in January 2009.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin v0.1 was the first release of Satoshi's software. He announced it on the Cryptography mailing list on 8 January 2009: “Announcing the first release of Bitcoin, a new electronic cash system that uses a peer-to-peer network to prevent double-spending.” It ran on Windows only for the time being and included the C++ source code (the announcement).

The release notes on bitcoin-list set out the rules that still apply, including the 21 million coin limit (release notes; see 21 million supply cap).

sections.html: Hal Finney ran it immediately, and Satoshi sent him the first transaction on 12 January. Within days Finney, Dustin Trammell and others were reporting bugs, and Satoshi shipped versions 0.1.2, 0.1.3 and 0.1.5 over the following weeks (v0.1.2). He also wrote to Wei Dai that the release “achieves nearly all the goals you set out to solve in your b-money paper”.

articles.title: Bitcoin white paper
articles.caption: “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System”
articles.short: The paper that described Bitcoin, announced 31 October 2008.
info: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
Electronic Cash Without a Trusted Third Party
articles.lead: The Bitcoin white paper, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, proposes “a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash” in which a peer-to-peer network prevents double-spending by timestamping transactions into a chain of proof-of-work.[1] Satoshi announced it on 31 October 2008.[2]

sections.html: In August 2008 Satoshi described the paper to Adam Back under the working title Electronic Cash Without a Trusted Third Party and offered a pre-release draft (the email). He asked Wei Dai for the date of b-money so he could cite it. nakamoto-archive keeps a version of the paper dated 3 October 2008.[3]

Satoshi posted to the Cryptography mailing list: “I've been working on a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.” He listed the main properties, starting with “Double-spending is prevented with a peer-to-peer network.” (the announcement). The first reply, from James A. Donald, questioned whether it could scale. The paper is hosted at bitcoin.org.[1]
The paper cites eight works, among them Wei Dai's b-money and Adam Back's Hashcash. It does not cite Nick Szabo's bit gold.[1] See Precursors of Bitcoin.

refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, bitcoin.org.
History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: bitcoin-list
articles.caption: The project's SourceForge mailing list
articles.short: Bitcoin's own announcement list on SourceForge, opened December 2008.
articles.label: bitcoin-list
articles.lead:
bitcoin-list was the project's mailing list on SourceForge. Satoshi opened it with a welcome message on 10 December 2008 and used it for release announcements and alerts until 2010 (open the label).

It carried the v0.1 release notes, the 0.3 announcement (“Escape the arbitrary inflation risk of centrally managed currencies! Bitcoin's total circulation is limited to 21 million coins.”) and, on 15 August 2010, the warning about the value overflow incident (0.3 announcement, the alert).

articles.title: bitcoin.org
articles.caption: Registered 18 August 2008
articles.short: The website Satoshi registered in 2008 to host the white paper and software.
info: The white paper and software downloads
articles.lead:
bitcoin.org is the domain Satoshi registered on 18 August 2008, ten weeks before the white paper.[1] It hosts the paper,[2] and in 2009 Martti Malmi worked on its pages with Satoshi (their emails).

A copy of the site from 3 March 2009 is kept in nakamoto-archive.[3] The bitcoin.org repository on GitHub, which holds release announcements and network alerts from 2011 onward, is also part of this dataset.

Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, bitcoin.org.
nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: BitcoinTalk
articles.caption: The Bitcoin forum Satoshi founded
articles.short: The forum Satoshi opened in November 2009, where he wrote most of his public posts.
articles.label: bitcointalk
articles.lead:
BitcoinTalk is the Bitcoin forum Satoshi created on 22 November 2009[1] with the post “Welcome to the new Bitcoin forum!” (the post). Martti Malmi set up the software (the emails).

Most of what Satoshi wrote in public is here: design explanations, release notes, bug reports and arguments with early users, from late 2009 until 12 December 2010 (his last post). In Satoshi Mail the forum threads are under the Forums tab (open Forums).
refs: Bitcointalk, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Blocktrainer archive
articles.caption: “Satoshi Nakamoto’s Emails & Posts: The Full Archive”
articles.short: Blocktrainer's searchable archive of Satoshi's emails and posts, with German translations.
articles.lead: Blocktrainer archive is the name used here for “Satoshi Nakamoto’s Emails & Posts: The Full Archive”, a searchable collection published by Blocktrainer. It brings together Satoshi's emails, forum posts and mailing-list contributions in date order, links each one to its original source, includes posts by early correspondents and forum users where they give context, and offers a German translation of every entry.[1]

sections.html:
On 20 October 2026 its 4,236 entries were checked against Satoshi Mail's data, and every one of them is also here. Its forum and mailing-list entries match the Satoshi Nakamoto Institute's collection post for post: 3,831 BitcoinTalk posts in 259 threads, 14 P2P Foundation posts and 72 mailing-list emails. Its private emails match nakamoto-archive's, except that it has no emails with Adam Back and includes only Satoshi's side of his exchanges with Mike Hearn and Dustin Trammell.

It dates Satoshi's email to Laszlo Hanyecz 11 December 2009, where nakamoto-archive's source gives May 2010 (the email). Conversations in Satoshi Mail that it includes link to it.

refs: Satoshi Nakamoto’s Emails & Posts: The Full Archive, Blocktrainer. Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Craig Wright
articles.caption: Claimed to be Satoshi; a UK court found he is not
articles.short: Australian who claimed to be Satoshi until a UK court ruled against him in 2024.
articles.lead: Craig Wright is an Australian computer scientist who claimed from 2016 to be Satoshi Nakamoto. The High Court in London ruled in 2024 that he is not.[1]

sections.html: In December 2015 Wired and Gizmodo suggested that Wright might be Satoshi.[2] On 2 May 2016 a post on his website associated him with Satoshi.[1] Gavin Andresen and Jon Matonis backed the claim; Jeff Garzik and Peter Todd disputed it.[2] In April 2019 he registered US copyrights in the white paper and the v0.1 code, and he sued people who accused him of lying about inventing Bitcoin.[1]

The Crypto Open Patent Alliance (COPA) sued Wright in London's High Court. After a five-week trial, Mr Justice Mellor ruled in March 2024 that Wright is not Satoshi Nakamoto. The written judgment, released on 20 May 2024, found that the documents he relied on were forgeries and that he had “lied to the court extensively and repeatedly”.[1] In December 2024 he received a suspended prison sentence for contempt of court, for violating a court order related to his claims.[2]

refs: Craig Steven Wright, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Cryptography mailing list
articles.caption: metzdowd.com
articles.short: The mailing list where Satoshi announced the white paper and v0.1.
articles.label: cryptography
articles.lead:
The Cryptography mailing list, hosted at metzdowd.com, is the list Satoshi used to announce the white paper on 31 October 2008 and v0.1 on 8 January 2009.

The white-paper thread is the first public discussion of Bitcoin. Members including James A. Donald, Ray Dillinger and Hal Finney debated its scalability, its incentives and its defence against attack, and Satoshi answered at length (the thread). It is under the Cryptography label in Satoshi Mail (open the label).

articles.title: Departure of Satoshi Nakamoto
articles.caption: December 2010 – April 2011
articles.short: How Satoshi withdrew from Bitcoin between December 2010 and April 2011.
articles.lead: Satoshi withdrew from Bitcoin gradually between December 2010 and April 2011, handing the project to Gavin Andresen and other developers.

sections.html: His last forum post, on 12 December 2010, announced version 0.3.19 and its denial-of-service limits (the post). It came a day after his warning that “WikiLeaks has kicked the hornet's nest” (WikiLeaks and Bitcoin). His last commit followed on 15 December (r202).

He kept writing privately into 2011. To Mike Hearn, on 23 April 2011: “I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.” (the email). To Andresen, on 26 April 2011, with the alert key: “I've moved on to other things and will probably be unavailable.” (the email). This archive holds no later email from him.

articles.title: Dustin Trammell
articles.caption: Early Bitcoin user
articles.short: Early user who emailed Satoshi in the first weeks of Bitcoin.
articles.label: dustin-trammell
articles.lead:
Dustin Trammell is an early Bitcoin user who ran the software within days of v0.1 and exchanged 22 emails with Satoshi in January 2009.

His first email reported that his node had generated coins but showed a zero credit, and pointed Satoshi to a public timestamping service (“Re: Bitcoin v0.1 released”). Later threads cover his ideas for the software and a test transfer (“A few thoughts...”, “BitCoin Transfer”). Satoshi wrote from satoshi@vistomail.com throughout.

Trammell published the exchange on his website, and nakamoto-archive keeps a copy.[1]
refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: First bitcoin transaction
articles.caption: 10 BTC from Satoshi to Hal Finney
articles.short: Satoshi's 10-bitcoin payment to Hal Finney in block 170.
articles.lead: The first bitcoin transaction was a payment of 10 bitcoins from Satoshi to Hal Finney, included in block 170 on 12 January 2009.[1] Finney had been running v0.1 since its release, and the two were exchanging bug reports at the time (their emails).
refs: History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Gavin Andresen
articles.caption: Satoshi's successor as lead developer
articles.short: Developer Satoshi handed the project and the alert key to.
info: Lead developer after Satoshi; the Bitcoin Faucet
articles.lead: Gavin Andresen is a software developer who discovered Bitcoin in 2010, created the Bitcoin Faucet website that gave bitcoin away, and became lead developer after Satoshi left.[1] His first forum posts in this archive date from June 2010 (his messages).

sections.html: Satoshi gave Andresen control of the source code repository and the network alert key.[2] On 26 April 2011 he sent him the alert key and broadcast code “in case you need it”, with a request: “I wish you wouldn't keep talking about me as a mysterious shadowy figure, the press just turns that into a pirate currency angle.” Andresen published the exchange on his website eleven years later (the email).[3] It is the latest email from Satoshi in this archive.
In 2014 Andresen stepped back as lead maintainer. His commit access was later revoked after he stated that Craig Wright was Satoshi; he later said it had been a mistake to trust Wright.[1]

refs: Gavin Andresen, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Genesis block
articles.caption: Block 0, dated 3 January 2009
articles.short: The first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, carrying a Times headline.
info: The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks
articles.lead:
The genesis block is block 0 of the Bitcoin blockchain, hard-coded into the software and dated 3 January 2009. Embedded in it is the text “The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks”.[1]

The headline serves as a timestamp, and has been read as a derisive comment on the instability caused by fractional-reserve banking.[2] Satoshi described it as “a hardcoded block that you start out with” (the post).

The first open-source client, v0.1, was released on 9 January 2009.[3] Satoshi saw newspapers as natural timestamps: in January 2009 he told Dustin Trammell that publishing hashes in “a magazine or newspaper” would “work a lot easier in court” (the email).

Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Hal Finney
articles.caption: Cypherpunk and the first Bitcoin user after Satoshi
articles.short: Cypherpunk who ran Bitcoin from its first release and received its first transaction.
articles.label: hal-finney
info: PGP Corporation, RPOW, the first bitcoin transaction
articles.lead: Hal Finney (1956–2014) was an American software developer and cypherpunk who worked for the PGP Corporation and in 2004 created the first reusable proof-of-work system, RPOW.[1] He was the first person other than Satoshi to use the Bitcoin software,[2] and on 12 January 2009 he received 10 bitcoins from Satoshi in block 170, the first bitcoin transaction.[3]

sections.html:
Finney was one of the reviewers who received Satoshi's source files in November 2008. His reply asks how large the network might grow: “Tens of nodes? Thousands? Millions?” (the email). Satoshi answered that 100,000 block-generating nodes was “a good ballpark large-scale size to think about”.

When v0.1 came out in January 2009, Finney ran it at once and spent the following days reporting crashes and testing debug builds with Satoshi (“Crash in bitcoin 0.1.0”, “select failed 10038 fix”). He later posted on the forum as Hal (his posts).

Finney announced in 2009 that he had been diagnosed with ALS. In March 2013 he wrote “Bitcoin and Me” on BitcoinTalk, describing his early involvement. He died on 28 August 2014 and was cryopreserved by the Alcor Life Extension Foundation.[1]

Finney was suggested as Satoshi, partly because he had lived for ten years in the same town as Dorian Nakamoto; he denied it.[1] The 2026 documentary Finding Satoshi proposed that Satoshi was a partnership between Finney and Len Sassaman.[2] Both have died, so neither can answer. See Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto.

refs: Hal Finney (computer scientist), Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto
articles.caption: An open question since 2008
articles.short: Who has been named as Satoshi, by whom, and how they responded.
articles.lead: The identity of Satoshi Nakamoto has never been established. Satoshi gave few personal details, used anonymous email services (Satoshi's accounts and keys), and stopped writing in 2011. The name might belong to a team of people.[1]

sections.html: On his P2P Foundation profile he claimed to be a 37-year-old man living in Japan. His writing uses British spellings, and his forum posts drop to almost none between 5 and 11 a.m. GMT (writing style).[1] The one later message attributed to his account reads, in full: “I am not Dorian Nakamoto.” (the post).

Each person below was publicly suggested as Satoshi, by others or, in one case, by himself. None has proven it.[1]

PersonSuggested byResponse
Hal FinneySpeculation after the 2014 Newsweek story; Finding Satoshi (2026)Denied before his death in 2014
Nick SzaboStylometric analysis (2013); New York Times (2015)Denied
Adam BackFinancial Times (2016); New York Times (2026)Denied
Len SassamanBitcoinTalk user (2013); Evan Hatch (2021); Finding Satoshi (2026)Died 2011
Peter ToddMoney Electric, HBO (2024)Denied
Dorian NakamotoNewsweek (2014)Denied
Craig WrightHimself, from 2016Court ruled he is not Satoshi (2024)

Others suggested include David Chaum, Paul Le Roux and Wei Dai.[1]
Proposed proofs include signing a message with the key associated with the first bitcoins, or moving the earliest bitcoins mined (Satoshi's coins).[1]

refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: James A. Donald
articles.caption: First public reply to the white paper
articles.short: Wrote the first public reply to the white paper.
info: First public reply to the white paper (2 November 2008)
articles.lead:
James A. Donald took part in the Cryptography mailing list. Two days after Satoshi posted the white paper he wrote the first public reply: “We very, very much need such a system, but the way I understand your proposal, it does not seem to scale to the required size.” (the thread). Satoshi's answers in that thread are some of his earliest explanations of how Bitcoin would scale.

Donald was also copied on Satoshi's November 2008 pre-release source code, along with Hal Finney and Ray Dillinger.

articles.title: Jeff Garzik
articles.caption: Prolific poster in Satoshi's forum threads
articles.short: Developer active in Satoshi's forum threads in 2010.
articles.lead:
Jeff Garzik is a software developer who, as jgarzik, is one of the most frequent posters in the forum threads Satoshi took part in (his messages). Through 2010 he proposed patches and features there, such as “[PATCH] increase block size limit” (the thread).

Garzik was among those who disputed Craig Wright's claim to be Satoshi.[1]
refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Jon Matonis
articles.caption: Received an email from Satoshi in 2010
articles.short: Early advocate who corresponded with Satoshi in 2010.
articles.lead:
Jon Matonis corresponded with Satoshi in early 2010. The archive holds the last email Satoshi sent him, dated 4 March 2010, which was later posted on the Bitcoin Foundation forum (the email).[1]

Matonis was one of those who backed Craig Wright's claim to be Satoshi.[2]
refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Laszlo Hanyecz
articles.caption: Bought two pizzas for 10,000 BTC
articles.short: Programmer who made the first known commercial bitcoin transaction.
info: Bitcoin Pizza Day; the Mac OS X port; GPU mining
articles.lead: Laszlo Hanyecz is a programmer who on 22 May 2010 paid 10,000 bitcoins for two Papa John's pizzas, the first known commercial transaction with bitcoin (Bitcoin Pizza Day).[1]

sections.html: Hanyecz ported the client to Mac OS X; Satoshi's release notes for version 0.3 list “Mac OS X version (thanks to Laszlo)” (the 0.3 announcement). He posted on the forum as laszlo.

He was also mining with a graphics card. In May 2010 Satoshi asked him to hold back, arguing that GPUs would concentrate new coins among a few people too early: “I don't mean to sound like a socialist, I don't care if wealth is concentrated, but for now, we get more growth by giving that money to 100% of the people than giving it to 20%.” (the email). The email later surfaced in a Reddit thread, the source of nakamoto-archive's copy.[2]

refs: Bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: Len Sassaman
articles.caption: Maintainer of the Mixmaster remailer
articles.short: Remailer developer proposed as Satoshi, or part of him.
articles.lead:
Len Sassaman was the maintainer of the Mixmaster anonymous remailer code.[1] He died in July 2011, a few months after the last email from Satoshi in this archive. A tribute to him was embedded in the Bitcoin blockchain.[2]

Sassaman does not appear in Satoshi's correspondence. A BitcoinTalk user suggested him as Satoshi in 2013, and developer Evan Hatch proposed him in 2021.[1] The 2026 documentary Finding Satoshi proposed that Satoshi was a partnership between Sassaman and Hal Finney.[2] Neither man can respond. See Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto.
refs: Len Sassaman, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Martti Malmi
articles.caption: Bitcoin's second developer, known as sirius
articles.short: Finnish developer who joined Satoshi in 2009 and built the website and forum.
articles.label: martti-malmi
articles.lead: Martti Malmi, known online as sirius, is a developer from Finland who volunteered to help Satoshi in May 2009. He exchanged more emails with Satoshi than anyone else in this archive.

sections.html:
Malmi wrote to Satoshi in May 2009 after promoting Bitcoin on a forum. Satoshi replied that “your understanding of bitcoin is spot on” and asked for help: “What we need most right now is website writing. My writing is not that great, I'm a much better coder.” (the conversation).

Over the next two years Malmi worked on the bitcoin.org website and FAQ, set up the forum that became BitcoinTalk (“Forum”) and organised translations (“Translation”). In December 2009 he told Satoshi he planned a small exchange service that would take PayPal at first (the email). They corresponded until February 2011.
Malmi published the emails on his own GitHub page, and nakamoto-archive keeps a copy.[1] Satoshi Mail shows them under his label (open the label).

refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: Media investigations
articles.caption: From Newsweek (2014) to Finding Satoshi (2026)
articles.short: Major journalistic attempts to unmask Satoshi, from Newsweek to Finding Satoshi.
articles.lead: Journalists and filmmakers have repeatedly tried to identify Satoshi. None of their candidates has been confirmed.

sections.html: On 6 March 2014 Newsweek published Leah McGrath Goodman's report identifying Dorian Nakamoto, a man living in Temple City, California, as Bitcoin's creator.[1] He denied it, and the story was widely criticised.[2] The next day Satoshi's dormant P2P Foundation account posted “I am not Dorian Nakamoto.” (the post). The Satoshi Nakamoto Institute notes that its authenticity “demands scrutiny”: the account was compromised through an email hack in September 2014, though there is no clear sign it was compromised when this post was made.[3]
In December 2015 both publications suggested that Craig Wright might be Satoshi.[2] A UK court found in 2024 that he is not.
Cullen Hoback's 2024 HBO documentary Money Electric: The Bitcoin Mystery named Peter Todd, who called the claim “ludicrous”.[4]

In April 2026 the New York Times published an investigation by John Carreyrou asserting that Adam Back is Satoshi. It cited his use of less common phrases, shared niche interests, and the timing of Satoshi's last communication and Back's first public comment on Bitcoin. Back denied it.[5]
The 2026 documentary Finding Satoshi proposed that Satoshi was a partnership between Len Sassaman and Hal Finney.[2] Both died years before the film.

articles.title: Mike Hearn
articles.caption: Developer who received Satoshi's “moved on” email
articles.short: Developer who corresponded with Satoshi from 2009 to 2011 and wrote bitcoinj.
articles.label: mike-hearn
info: BitCoinJ, a Java implementation of Bitcoin
articles.lead: Mike Hearn is a software developer who wrote to Satoshi in April 2009, while working at Google (“We use them here at Google for everything”), and kept corresponding with him until April 2011 (their emails).

sections.html:
His first email opened: “I read your paper on BitCoin with great interest. I found it a bit confusing though”. He asked how one chain could scale, and where the figure of 24 million coins came from (“Questions about BitCoin”). Satoshi's answer compared Bitcoin to the Visa network, which then processed about 15 million Internet purchases a day.

Their last exchange, in April 2011, contains Satoshi's line about leaving: “I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.” In the same email Satoshi hoped Hearn's Java client, bitcoinj, would keep developing (the email).

In March 2011 Hearn told Satoshi he had got “all the lawyers happy enough to release BitCoinJ under the Google name using the Apache 2 license” (the email).

Hearn published his emails with Satoshi on his website, and nakamoto-archive keeps copies.[1]

refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: Monuments to Satoshi
articles.caption: Budapest and Lugano
articles.short: Statues of Satoshi in Budapest and Lugano.
articles.lead:
Satoshi has been commemorated with statues.[1]

  • Budapest: a bust of Satoshi was installed in Budapest, Hungary, in 2021.[1]
  • Lugano: a statue by Valentina Picozzi in Lugano, Switzerland. It was stolen and thrown into the lake, and later recovered.[1]
refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: nakamoto-archive
articles.caption: github.com/lugaxker/nakamoto-archive
articles.short: A GitHub archive of Satoshi's writings and primary sources, including private email.
info: 44 source files, each with a SHA-256 hash
articles.lead:
nakamoto-archive is a GitHub repository that collects Satoshi's writings together with the primary sources they come from: mailing-list archives, the email collections of Martti Malmi, Mike Hearn, Dustin Trammell and Hal Finney, the emails with Adam Back and Wei Dai, early code, and an early version of bitcoin.org.[1] Each source file is listed with its date, origin and SHA-256 hash.

Satoshi Mail's Private tab is built from it (open Private).
refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: New Liberty Standard
articles.caption: Early exchanger and price-setter
articles.short: Pseudonymous early user who published a bitcoin exchange rate.
articles.lead:
New Liberty Standard is the pseudonym of an early Bitcoin user who published an exchange rate for bitcoin. In February 2010 he explained on the forum: “I use a formula to calculate my exchange rate which is described on my exchange rate page” (the thread).

He is one of the most active participants in Satoshi's threads (his messages).

articles.title: Nick Szabo
articles.caption: Proposer of bit gold and smart contracts
articles.short: Computer scientist who proposed bit gold and smart contracts.
articles.lead:
Nick Szabo is a computer scientist and legal scholar who wrote about smart contracts in the 1990s and in 1998 designed bit gold, a mechanism for a decentralised digital currency.[1] Bit gold is one of Bitcoin's precursors, although the white paper does not cite it.[2]

Szabo does not appear in Satoshi's correspondence. In December 2013 a stylometric analysis by Skye Grey linked him to the white paper,[3] and in 2015 Nathaniel Popper of the New York Times pointed to him. He has repeatedly denied being Satoshi.[1] The Satoshi Nakamoto Institute keeps a large collection of his essays in its library.
refs: Nick Szabo, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, bitcoin.org.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: P2P Foundation
articles.caption: Where Satoshi introduced Bitcoin to a wider audience
articles.short: The forum where Satoshi described Bitcoin for a general audience in February 2009.
articles.label: p2pfoundation
articles.lead:
On 11 February 2009 Satoshi posted “Bitcoin open source implementation of P2P currency” on its forum, his most accessible early description of the problem Bitcoin solves: trust in central banks and financial institutions (the post). He sent the same text to the P2P Research mailing list (the email).

On his P2P Foundation profile Satoshi claimed to be a 37-year-old man living in Japan.[1] The same thread received the post “I am not Dorian Nakamoto” in March 2014 (Media investigations).
refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Peter Todd
articles.caption: Bitcoin developer named by HBO
articles.short: Bitcoin developer named as Satoshi by a 2024 HBO documentary; he denies it.
articles.lead: Peter Todd is a Canadian software developer and an early contributor to Bitcoin. Cullen Hoback's 2024 HBO documentary Money Electric: The Bitcoin Mystery named him as Satoshi. Todd denied it, calling the claim “ludicrous”.[1] He does not appear in Satoshi's correspondence. See Media investigations.
refs: Peter Todd (programmer), Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Pre-release source code
articles.caption: Satoshi's November 2008 code
articles.short: The earliest known Bitcoin code, sent to three reviewers in November 2008.
info: Hal Finney, Ray Dillinger, James A. Donald
articles.lead:
In November 2008, two months before the first release, Satoshi sent the core of his source code to three people from the Cryptography mailing list: Hal Finney, Ray Dillinger and James A. Donald. Finney's reply, copied to the other two, is in this archive (the email).

Dillinger later published the main files on BitcoinTalk, and nakamoto-archive keeps a copy.[1]
refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: Precursors of Bitcoin
articles.caption: Ecash, Hashcash, b-money, bit gold and RPOW
articles.short: The digital-cash ideas Bitcoin built on.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin combined ideas that cryptographers had been developing for two decades. Satoshi said as much to Adam Back when he learned of b-money: “my ideas start from exactly that point.” (the email).

  • Ecash (1983): David Chaum's anonymous cryptographic electronic money, using blind signatures; the money was cryptographically signed by a bank.[1]
  • Hashcash (1997): Adam Back's proof-of-work scheme for spam control.[2] The white paper cites it.[3]
  • b-money (1998): Wei Dai's “anonymous, distributed electronic cash system”.[4] It is reference [1] in the white paper.[3]
  • Bit gold (1998): Nick Szabo's mechanism for a decentralised digital currency.[5]
  • RPOW (2004): Hal Finney's reusable proof-of-work system, the first of its kind.[6]

The white paper presents its own answer as a solution to “the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network”.[3]

articles.title: Ray Dillinger
articles.caption: Reviewer of the November 2008 code
articles.short: Reviewed Satoshi's code in 2008 and later published it.
articles.lead:
Ray Dillinger took part in the Cryptography mailing list discussion of the white paper and was one of three people Satoshi sent his source files to in November 2008, along with Hal Finney and James A. Donald. He was copied as bear@sonic.net (Finney's reply).

Dillinger, posting as Cryddit, later published the main files from that November 2008 code on BitcoinTalk; nakamoto-archive keeps a copy[1] (Pre-release source code).
refs: nakamoto-archive, “Complete archive of Satoshi Nakamoto's writings and productions”, GitHub. The README lists each source file with its origin, date and SHA-256 hash.

articles.title: Satoshi (unit)
articles.caption: 0.00000001 BTC
articles.short: Bitcoin's smallest unit, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin.
articles.lead:
A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin: one hundred-millionth (0.00000001) of a coin.[1]

Satoshi explained the eight decimal places in 2010: “It shows 1.00 but internally it's 1.00000000.” (the post).
refs: Bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Satoshi Nakamoto
articles.caption: The name signed to the Bitcoin white paper
articles.short: The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin.
info: Designing Bitcoin; writing its white paper and first software
articles.lead:
Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin, wrote the white paper that describes it, and released its first software.[1] Between August 2008 and April 2011 Satoshi corresponded through mailing lists, forums and private email, made every change to the original client himself until mid-2010, and then stopped. Who was behind the name has never been established.[1]

This archive collects his known emails, forum posts and commits. Satoshi Mail opens his inbox; this article summarises what the messages show.

sections.html:
Satoshi registered the domain bitcoin.org on 18 August 2008.[1] Two days later he wrote to Adam Back to check how to cite Hashcash in “a paper that references your Hashcash paper” (the emails), and Back pointed him to Wei Dai's b-money. Satoshi wrote to Dai the same week (the emails).

On 31 October 2008 he announced the paper on the Cryptography mailing list: “I've been working on a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.” (the announcement). In November he sent early source files to Hal Finney, Ray Dillinger and James A. Donald. The genesis block is dated 3 January 2009, and Bitcoin v0.1 followed that month.

Until mid-2010 Satoshi made all changes to the code himself,[1] committing to the SourceForge repository and announcing releases on bitcoin-list. He recruited Martti Malmi to write the website and FAQ, opened the Bitcoin forum in November 2009, and from mid-2010 worked increasingly with Gavin Andresen.

He fixed the value overflow bug in August 2010 within hours,[2] added an alert system for emergencies, and in December 2010 asked WikiLeaks not to accept bitcoin (WikiLeaks and Bitcoin).

Satoshi's last forum post is dated 12 December 2010 and his last commit, SVN revision 202, 15 December 2010. In April 2011 he told Mike Hearn “I've moved on to other things”, and three days later sent Andresen the alert key (departure). In March 2014 the post “I am not Dorian Nakamoto” appeared on his P2P Foundation account; its authenticity is uncertain (Newsweek, 2014).

On his P2P Foundation profile Satoshi claimed to be a 37-year-old man living in Japan; it is widely doubted that he was Japanese.[1] His British spellings and posting hours have been read as clues (writing style). Many people have been publicly named as Satoshi and those named have denied it; a UK court ruled in 2024 that Craig Wright, who claimed the title, is not him. See Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto.

Estimates of the bitcoins in Satoshi's possession range from 750,000 to 1.1 million, untouched since 2010 (Satoshi's coins).[1] Bitcoin's smallest unit is called the satoshi,[3] and there are statues of him in Budapest and Lugano (monuments).

articles.title: Satoshi Nakamoto Institute
articles.caption: The source of this archive
articles.short: The organisation whose collection of Satoshi's writings is the core of this archive.
articles.lead:
The Satoshi Nakamoto Institute (SNI) was founded in November 2013 “to advance and preserve knowledge of Bitcoin's history, economics, and technology”.[1] Its Complete Satoshi collection of emails and forum posts, with the surrounding threads, is the core of Satoshi Mail.[2]

SNI also publishes The Quotable Satoshi, a library of papers and the Mempool essays.[1] It notes that the 2014 “I am not Dorian Nakamoto” post's authenticity “demands scrutiny”.[2] See The Quotable Satoshi and nakamoto-archive.
refs: About, Satoshi Nakamoto Institute.
The Complete Satoshi, Satoshi Nakamoto Institute.

articles.title: Satoshi's accounts and keys
articles.caption: Email addresses, handles and keys
articles.short: The email addresses, forum accounts and cryptographic keys Satoshi used.
articles.lead: Satoshi used several accounts, mostly through services that did not require a real identity.

sections.html:
• satoshi@anonymousspeech.com: his earliest address, used to write to Adam Back and Wei Dai in August 2008.
  • satoshi@vistomail.com: used to announce the white paper on the Cryptography list, bitcoin-list, and his emails with Hal Finney and Dustin Trammell.
  • satoshin@gmx.com: used from 2009 with Martti Malmi, Mike Hearn and Gavin Andresen. It is the address printed on the white paper at bitcoin.org.[1]

The archive's private emails show the split:

He posted as satoshi on BitcoinTalk, committed as s_nakamoto on SourceForge, and kept a profile on the P2P Foundation site. He published a PGP public key in 2008.[2] He also held the network alert key, which he passed to Gavin Andresen in April 2011 (the email).

In September 2014 his P2P Foundation account was compromised through an email hack.[3]

refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, bitcoin.org.

The Complete Satoshi, Satoshi Nakamoto Institute.

articles.title: Satoshi's coins
articles.caption: Estimated holdings, untouched since 2010
articles.short: The 750,000 to 1.1 million bitcoins attributed to Satoshi, untouched since 2010.
articles.lead:
Estimates of the bitcoins in Satoshi's possession range from 750,000 to 1.1 million; the wallet has been untouched since 2010.[1] Another estimate puts what he mined at about one million.[2]

Moving the earliest bitcoins mined, or signing a message with the key associated with them, has been proposed as proof of being Satoshi (Identity of Satoshi Nakamoto).[1] His 10-bitcoin payment to Hal Finney was the first bitcoin transaction.[3]

articles.title: Satoshi's writing style
articles.caption: Spelling, spacing and hours
articles.short: What Satoshi's spelling, punctuation and posting times reveal, measured from the archive.
articles.lead: Satoshi's writing has been studied closely for clues to his identity. Analyses point to British spellings, double-spaced sentences and a long daily gap in posting.[1] The figures below are computed live from the messages in this archive.

His writing includes British forms such as “colour”, “grey” and “maths”, and the phrase “bloody hard”,[1] though he also uses American spellings.

articles.title: SourceForge
articles.caption: Bitcoin's first code host
articles.short: Where Bitcoin's code, releases and mailing list lived until 2011.
articles.lead:
Bitcoin's first home was SourceForge, which hosted the downloads, the bitcoin-list mailing list and a Subversion repository. Satoshi committed as s_nakamoto; the first revision credited to him is r15 on 21 October 2009 (r15) and his last is r202, “get external ip from irc”, on 15 December 2010 (r202). The archive lists 203 commits under his name (open Commits).

The SVN history was later imported into the Git repository on GitHub that became Bitcoin Core.[1]
refs: bitcoin/bitcoin, Bitcoin Core source repository, GitHub.

articles.title: The Quotable Satoshi
articles.caption: Quotes sorted into 25 topics
articles.short: SNI's collection of Satoshi quotes, which supplies the Topics in Satoshi Mail.
articles.lead:
The Quotable Satoshi is the Satoshi Nakamoto Institute's collection of short quotations from Satoshi's emails, posts and the white paper, each filed under topics such as mining, privacy and scalability.[1] In Satoshi Mail these categories are the Topics in the sidebar, and messages that contain a quote are marked.

articles.title: Value overflow incident
articles.caption: Block 74638, 15 August 2010
articles.short: The August 2010 bug that created over 184 billion bitcoins, fixed within hours.
info: Two outputs of over 92 billion BTC each
articles.lead: The value overflow incident was a bug found on 15 August 2010, when a transaction in block 74638 used an integer overflow to create bitcoins out of nothing: two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC each (the forum report). The bug was fixed within hours.[1]

sections.html:
Satoshi posted an alert within hours: “*** WARNING *** We are investigating a problem. DO NOT TRUST ANY TRANSACTIONS THAT HAPPENED AFTER 15.08.2010 17:05 UTC (block 74638) until the issue is resolved.” (the alert). He committed the fix the same day (“fix for block 74638 overflow output transaction”) and released version 0.3.10, which rejected the bad block (the release post).

Satoshi asked users to stop generating so a corrected branch could overtake the bad one. The next day he wrote: “It looks like we overtook the bad chain somewhere around 74689”, and added code to reorganise the chain automatically (the thread).
A week later Satoshi began building an alert system so that developers could warn every node of an emergency (the post). He later handed the alert key to Gavin Andresen.

refs: History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.

articles.title: Wei Dai
articles.caption: Author of b-money and Crypto++
articles.short: Computer engineer whose b-money is the white paper's first reference.
articles.label: wei-dai
articles.lead: Wei Dai is a computer engineer who in 1998 published “b-money, an anonymous, distributed electronic cash system”.[1] B-money is reference [1] in the white paper.[2]

sections.html: After Adam Back pointed him to b-money, Satoshi wrote to Dai in August 2008: “I was very interested to read your b-money page. I'm getting ready to release a paper that expands on your ideas into a complete working system.” He asked for the year of publication so he could cite it. In January 2009 he wrote again to say he had released v0.1, which he thought “achieves nearly all the goals you set out to solve in your b-money paper” (the emails).
Dai also wrote Crypto++, a C++ cryptography library first released in 1995.[1] In 2010 Satoshi added part of it to Bitcoin for a faster SHA-256 (SVN r114).

refs: Wei Dai, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, bitcoin.org.

articles.title: WikiLeaks and Bitcoin
articles.caption: “Kicked the hornet's nest”, December 2010
articles.short: Satoshi's December 2010 appeal to WikiLeaks not to use Bitcoin.
articles.lead:
In December 2010 forum users urged WikiLeaks to accept bitcoin. Satoshi disagreed: “No, don't ‘bring it on’. The project needs to grow gradually so the software can be strengthened along the way. I make this appeal to WikiLeaks not to try to use Bitcoin. Bitcoin is a small beta community in its infancy. You would not stand to get more than pocket change, and the heat you would bring would likely destroy us at this stage.” (the post).

When PC World linked Bitcoin to WikiLeaks a few days later, he wrote: “It would have been nice to get this attention in any other context. WikiLeaks has kicked the hornet's nest, and the swarm is headed towards us.” (the post). It was one of his last posts. WikiLeaks began accepting bitcoin in June 2011.[1]
refs: History of bitcoin, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Retrieved 20 October 2026.
